verses.text: Then David came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?”

David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me to do something, and has said to me, ‘Let no one know anything about the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you. I have sent the young men to a certain place.’
Now therefore what is under your hand? Please give me five loaves of bread in my hand, or whatever is available.”
The priest answered David, and said, “I have no common bread, but there is holy bread; if only the young men have kept themselves from women.”

David answered the priest, and said to him, “Truly, women have been kept from us as usual these three days. When I came out, the vessels of the young men were holy, though it was only a common journey. How much more then today shall their vessels be holy?”
So the priest gave him holy bread; for there was no bread there but the show bread that was taken from before Yahweh, to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away.
Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before Yahweh; and his name was Doeg the Edomite, the best of the herdsmen who belonged to Saul.
David said to Ahimelech, “Isn’t there here under your hand spear or sword? For I have neither brought my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s business required haste.”

The priest said, “Behold, the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the valley of Elah, is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you would like to take that, take it; for there is no other except that here.” David said, “There is none like that. Give it to me.”
David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, “Isn’t this David the king of the land? Didn’t they sing to one another about him in dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands?’”
David laid up these words in his heart, and was very afraid of Achish the king of Gath.
He changed his behavior before them, and pretended to be insane in their hands, and scribbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down on his beard.
Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you see the man is insane. Why then have you brought him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to play the madman in my presence? Should this fellow come into my house?”

footnotes.content: Ahimelech trembles at the sight of David alone. Even before David speaks, the priest reads the story in his bearing—fear, urgency, solitude. Sometimes those who serve the Lord learn to see sorrow in a stranger's silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks a half-truth shaped by fear. The king did send him—just not on the errand he describes. When we're desperate, our words curve to fit the shape of safety we're reaching for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What is under your hand?"—the ancient language of the needy speaking to the one with means. Five loaves. Not a feast, but the bread a running man needs. There is mercy in the simplicity of the request.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest's hesitation holds both law and love. The showbread belongs to the Lord's table alone—yet he thinks of the young men's hunger, and asks the question that might open a door between duty and compassion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks in the language of holiness, answering the priest's worry with the assurance of readiness. When need meets someone who guards both law and mercy, we find we know what to say to reach their better nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The showbread, kept before Yahweh's face, crosses into David's hands. The Lord's bread becomes food for the hunted. Ahimelech's choice—to break the holy for the sake of mercy—foreshadows a greater mercy yet to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Doeg stands detained in the sanctuary that day, Saul's herdsman, watching. He sees the priest give David bread and sword. This moment, unseen by David, will be reported, and Ahimelech's mercy will become his undoing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asks for a weapon with the same fear-shaped half-truth—the king's urgent business left him weaponless. But there is truth beneath it: a man in flight is always in a hurry, and always comes seeking what he lacks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Goliath's sword hangs wrapped in cloth behind the ephod—the blade of a giant David had given to the Lord as a trophy of grace. Now, in desperation, David takes back what he once surrendered. The sword knows both victories.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Nob to Gath—David flees to the land of his former enemy, carrying Goliath's sword. Fear is a strange guide: it leads us away from what we know toward what we once conquered, as if past victory could shelter us now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Achish's servants know him by fame—"Saul his thousands, David his ten thousands." The song that celebrated him becomes the very thing that threatens him. Glory, when we are hunted, becomes a noose we cannot slip.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David lays the servants' words in his heart and trembles. The man who killed Goliath now knows terror—not of giants, but of recognition. Fear teaches us how small we truly are, and how far a reputation can reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He feigns madness—scribbling walls, letting spittle fall, changing his shape to match the disguise. When we are hunted, we will reshape ourselves into anything the hunter expects to see. Yet the Lord knows the heart beneath the performance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Achish sees the madness and speaks with disdain—why bring such a broken man into his presence? The disguise works because Achish chooses to look away. Sometimes survival means accepting the shame of being seen as less than we are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Do I lack madmen?" Achish casts David out disguised as a fool. Readers today hear an echo: when we have been humbled, played the part of the broken or the fool to survive, the Lord has not forgotten us. He sees what others dismiss, and will restore what they reject.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
